newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich orders review of military services.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich orders review of military services.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich has ordered a congressional review to find out if instructors in other military services, not just the Army, have sexually abused female recruits, members of Congress said Thursday.

Gingrich asked leaders of the House National Security Committee to conduct the military-wide review in the wake of a growing scandal that hit Army training bases last month, committee members told reporters.

"It is critical for Congress to ensure that all allegations of abuse are aggressively investigated and that appropriate actions are taken by all military services to punish those responsible and to prevent such abuses in the future," Gingrich said in a letter to the committee.

Indiana Republican Stephen Buyer, a committee member, said the review will be conducted by the personnel subcommittee. Buyer and Florida Republican Representative Tillie Fowler said on Dec. 11 House members will visit Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland, where the Army's sex abuse scandal became public two weeks ago.
The Army said then that a captain and a drill sergeant faced charges including rape of recruits and that another drill sergeant had been charged with sexual misconduct.
Since then, seven drill instructors at Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri, have been charged with sexual misconduct and one of them has been discharged and sentenced to jail.
Other Army bases are also investigating allegations of misconduct by drill instructors.

The Defence Department said Thursday it had ordered the individual military services to come up with "uniform reporting techniques" on all types of crimes and offences, including rape and sexual harassment.

Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters that Congress had ordered the military services to do so in 1989 but had provided no money and that the department was just getting around to following the directive. He denied that the Pentagon order, which went out on Oct. 15 after the Army investigation began at Aberdeen, was prompted by the scandal.
"This is an issue that's been around for a while. It's frankly a deficiency. The department admits it's a deficiency," he said.

The Washington Post reported Friday that Army Secretary Togo West planned to announce he has asked the Army's inspector general to find out what the commanders at the Aberdeen Proving Ground knew about the alleged incidents of sexual abuse, including multiple rapes.
The probe also would look at whether the commanders contributed to creating an atmosphere that permitted or fostered such conduct, the newspaper said.
The Congress members said they particularly wanted to find out when they visit Aberdeen why victims were afraid or unwilling to report the sexual abuse.

"There were safeguards in place on paper that looked very good but in practice they were not working," Fowler said. "Why did these young women not feel that they had an avenue through which they could immediately report any untoward activity toward them?"
